clue.text: March followed by Queen perhaps hosting Republican politician

indicators.note: one thing followed by another means the second is placed straight after the first

parts.note: a demo is a protest march

indicators.note: a host takes a guest inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a queen is a female cat; 'perhaps' flags the example
standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A US political story: a protest march, a royal, and a Republican figure all in the same news item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' looks royal, but a queen is also a female cat. There is a joke too: a Republican sits inside the Democrat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Democrat is a member of one of the two major American parties, hence a politician.

clue.text: Loathe the essence of academic experiment

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of this eight-letter word
a test is an experiment

explanation.surface: Someone who hates the core of a scholarly experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Academic' has eight letters, so its essence is the central pair rather than a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to hate it intensely, a straightforward synonym for loathe.

clue.text: Sprouts ultimately moreish — or so mum's snarling!

indicators.note: snarling suggests something tangled and twisted, so the letters are jumbled
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of this word
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A child says Brussels sprouts are tasty while their mother growls about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprouts' looks like the vegetable, but it is a verb meaning grows fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that mushrooms expands rapidly, just as a business can be said to sprout up quickly.

clue.text: Actress Theron ignoring unknown goon

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Charlize Theron is a South African-born film actress
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z; this is the one removed

explanation.surface: An actress refusing to acknowledge a thug.
explanation.walkthrough: Take Z out of CHARLIZE. In British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words for a silly or stupid person, so a charlie is a goon.

clue.text: Wrong answer held up by schoolgirl

indicators.note: in a down entry, something held up rests on top of its support, so one piece sits above the other

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
a miss is a young girl

explanation.surface: A pupil holding up an incorrect answer in class.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, A 'held up by' MISS means A sits on top of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amiss is out of order or not right, the same as being wrong.

clue.text: Returned some swedes, palpably out of date

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so it reads backwards
some means a part of, so the letters are a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Taking back some turnips that were obviously past their sell-by date.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'swedes, palpably' read sweDES PALpably, then backwards for LAPSED. A swede is the British name for a rutabaga.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapsed membership or licence has expired, so it is no longer valid or current.

clue.text: Accessory to crime in area streets ahead

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
streets ahead is an idiom for much better

explanation.surface: A crime accomplice working in a neighbourhood far ahead of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Streets' suggests roads in the area; 'streets ahead' is one idiom, meaning far superior.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter helps or encourages someone committing an offence, which is exactly an accessory.

clue.text: One practising winter sport, Victor escapes layabout

indicators.note: whatever escapes gets out and is gone, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a skiver is British slang for someone who dodges work
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A winter sportsman named Victor runs away from an idler.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove V from SKIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A skier takes part in skiing, the classic snow sport of the cold season.

clue.text: Shows what negative theatre critics do

definitions.meaning: first meaning: puts on view, exhibits
second meaning, split in two: to dis is to disparage, and theatre critics review stage productions

explanation.surface: A wry remark on how harsh reviewers treat stage productions.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DIS PLAYS: 'dis' is slang for criticise disrespectfully.
explanation.definitionFit: To display something is to exhibit it, so shows works as a verb in the third person.

clue.text: Very involved, awfully keen on training editor brought up

indicators.note: in a down entry, being on something means sitting above it, so the parts are joined in order
awfully means badly, so these letters are messed up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing letters up makes them read from bottom to top

parts.note: PE is physical education, school training
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A deeply committed, enthusiastic trainee raised by an editor.
explanation.walkthrough: KNEE from KEEN, then PE plus ED read upwards gives DEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Being knee-deep in something means heavily immersed or entangled in it, an idiom for deep involvement.

clue.text: Marsupials, wild native animals circling daughter and son

indicators.note: to circle something is to go round it, so letters surround others
wild means out of control, so these letters run loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Wild Australian creatures surrounding a family's children.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle NATIVE ANIMALS into TASMANIAN EVIL, then D and S slot in: TASMANIAN D EVIL S.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmanian devils are carnivorous pouched mammals found only on the island of Tasmania.

clue.text: Ambles in front of sickeningly provocative posters

indicators.note: being in front of means coming first, so the parts join in that order

parts.note: the opening letter of this word
trolls post inflammatory messages online to provoke

explanation.surface: Someone walks past nasty online provocateurs.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no explicit 'first' signal: the first letter of 'sickeningly' is taken as it is the word placed 'in front of'. 'Posters' are people who post online, not placards.
explanation.definitionFit: To stroll is to walk in a slow, relaxed way, the same leisurely pace as amble.

clue.text: Have Spellbound rental playing for husband to get into

indicators.note: to get into something is to go inside it
playing about with something rearranges it freely

parts.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Hiring out the Hitchcock film Spellbound for a husband to watch.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes Spellbound look like the film title; 'Have spellbound' is the definition. RENTAL is shuffled to ENTRAL and H goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To enthral someone is to captivate them completely, holding them as if under a spell.

clue.text: Darling Auntie brushing off second black insect

parts.note: honey is a term of endearment

indicators.note: to brush something off is to sweep it away, so a letter is lost

parts.note: Auntie and the Beeb are both British nicknames for the BBC
B is black, as on pencils; it is the later of the two Bs that goes

explanation.surface: A beloved aunt flicking away an insect for the second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auntie' is not a relative: it is a fond British nickname for the BBC, which is also called the Beeb.
explanation.definitionFit: The honey bee is a familiar species kept in hives for its sweet product, an insect.

clue.text: Spooner's enjoyable snack for tea party

indicators.note: Rev Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

parts.note: something enjoyable is fun; it takes the B from the other word
a snack is a bite; it takes the F from the other word

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark about a pleasant snack served at tea.
explanation.walkthrough: FUN BITE with F and B swapped. A bunfight is a jocular British term for a tea party or similar gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunfight is informal British humour for a social tea gathering, where buns are eaten.

clue.text: Largely bad-tempered, yelled on vacation, turning red

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not wholly, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: rude here means ill-mannered and surly

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so letters read backwards
a vacated house is emptied, so only the outside letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters only

explanation.surface: A furious person shouting on holiday and going red in the face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like a holiday but means emptied; 'turning red' looks like the definition, but 'turning' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddy describes a healthy reddish complexion, so it is an adjective meaning red.

clue.text: Stumbling on to nudes, become incensed

indicators.note: stumbling means tripping and falling into disorder, so letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tripping onto naked people and getting outraged.
explanation.walkthrough: Do one's nut is British slang for losing one's temper; the apostrophe is not shown in the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: To do one's nut is an informal British idiom for getting extremely angry or furious.

clue.text: Change gear here with possible dip ahead?

definitions.text: Change gear here with possible dip ahead?

parts.words: Change gear here with possible dip ahead?
parts.note: surface reading: shifting a car's gears before the road drops

parts.words: Change gear here with possible dip ahead?
parts.note: setter's reading: a seaside cabin where you change clothes before a swim

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gear' means clothing and a 'dip' is a quick swim, not a motoring hazard.
explanation.definitionFit: A small wooden shelter on the shore lets bathers put on swimming costumes before entering the sea.

clue.text: Racecourse records form regularly

parts.note: EPs are extended-play records

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A racing venue keeping track of horses' form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Records' and 'form' sound like racing statistics; they are discs and a word to thin out. Epsom is the Surrey course that hosts the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs is a famous English horse-racing venue, home of the Derby.

clue.text: Violinist's bill of fare, limitless thing

parts.note: a bill of fare is a menu

indicators.note: without limits means without edges, so only the inner letters stay

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A musician's dinner menu, described as something endless.
explanation.walkthrough: Yehudi Menuhin was a celebrated twentieth-century violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: Yehudi Menuhin was among the most famous concert fiddle players of his era.

clue.text: Sleep with ring on, embracing the French emperor

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms around, so letters enclose others

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep
O is ring-shaped
taken as written
le is the masculine French word for the

explanation.surface: A ruler going to bed still wearing his ring, hugging someone from France.
explanation.walkthrough: NAP, then O and ON wrapping LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself ruler of the French Empire in 1804.

clue.text: Cricketer's PIN error

parts.note: pins is informal for legs
a slip is a small mistake

explanation.surface: A cricket player mistyping a bank card number.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make PIN look like a bank code; it is a leg. Leg slip is a cricket fielding position behind the batsman on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: Leg slip names both a fielding position and, by extension, the player stationed there.

clue.text: Visiting court, fail to find cupboard

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so letters sit within others

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court
to lose is to fail to win

explanation.surface: Someone at a courthouse who cannot locate a storage space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court or tennis court, but only its standard abbreviation is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A closet is a cupboard or small storage room, chiefly the American term.

clue.text: What noisy soccer fans may do around one — start to imbibe drink

indicators.note: going around something encloses it

parts.words: What noisy soccer fans may do
parts.note: football crowds chant
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Rowdy football supporters gathering round to start drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: CHANT holds I, then the first letter of 'imbibe' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is a red wine from Tuscany, so it is an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Prelude in Fortnite getting a twist

indicators.note: a twist turns something round, so the letters face the other way
in means inside, so the letters lie within the following word

parts.note: the letters inside this word

explanation.surface: The opening of the video game Fortnite has a plot twist.
explanation.walkthrough: fORTNIte read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is an introduction or opening passage, the same idea as a prelude.

clue.text: I'm not impressed at first by Italian gelato portion

indicators.note: at first means at the beginning, so initial letters are taken

parts.note: the first letters of these three words
a deal is an amount, as in a great deal

explanation.surface: Someone unimpressed by a serving of Italian ice cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like it belongs to the definition, but it signals initial letters of the following three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'big deal' sarcastically is a dismissive exclamation showing one is unimpressed.

clue.text: Slow part of snooker match broadcast

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than read, so the sound matters

parts.note: a break is a player's scoring run in snooker

explanation.surface: A tediously slow stretch of a televised snooker game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slow' looks like describing the match, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To brake is to reduce speed using a vehicle's stopping mechanism, so to slow down.

clue.text: Drunk inhaled his teeth and got media attention!

indicators.note: a drunk person is all over the place, so letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunk swallowed his dentures and became front-page news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like the subject of the sentence; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitting the headlines means becoming prominent news, attracting sudden press coverage.

clue.text: Troublesome Spike wacky at the end

parts.note: a thorn is a sharp spike on a plant

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A difficult character called Spike behaving oddly at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes Spike look like a name, such as Spike Milligan.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorny issue is a difficult, tricky one, full of complications and problems.

clue.text: Persevere with American singer going after retro look

indicators.note: going after means following, so the parts join in that order
retro means looking backwards, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: a peek is a quick look
A is the abbreviation for American
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: An American vocalist chasing an old-fashioned image.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'singer' is a bird, not a performer: a tit is a common British songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep at it is to continue working steadily despite difficulty, which is persevering.
